subject: physics
question_text: Explain Stokes' law with an application.

mark_split.label: Why the impact speed is moderate

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 10 Short Answer Question 10 (printed p.110). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The four-way mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: Stokes' law F = 6πηrv holds for a small sphere moving slowly with streamline flow around it; for a falling raindrop the drag grows with speed until it balances weight minus upthrust, 6πηrv = (4/3)πr³(ρ − σ)g, giving the terminal velocity v_t = (2/9)r²g(ρ − σ)/η, arithmetic of the balance verified.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: Stokes' law
lines: Stokes' law: a small sphere of
radius r moving slowly with
velocity v through a fluid of
coefficient of viscosity η meets a
viscous drag
provided the flow around the
sphere stays streamline.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Write the formula and name every symbol.
steps.why: The condition — small sphere, slow motion, streamline flow — is part of the law itself: the formula does not hold once the flow around the sphere turns turbulent.
common_mistakes: Writing the formula without naming r, η and v.

recall.must_convey: That Stokes' law gives the viscous drag on a small sphere as F = 6 pi eta r v, for streamline flow around it.
accept: F equals 6 pi eta r v
viscous drag on a small sphere

steps.memory_tip: F = 6πηrv — small sphere, slow motion, streamline flow around it.

steps.label: Forces on a raindrop
lines: Application — a falling raindrop.
As it falls it is acted on by its
weight downward, the upthrust of
the air upward, and the viscous
drag upward, which grows larger as
its speed increases.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Name all three forces, and say the drag grows with speed.
steps.why: Setting out the three forces, and noting that only the drag changes with speed, is what makes the next step — the balance — possible.
common_mistakes: Naming only weight and drag, leaving out the upthrust of the air.
Saying the drag is constant; it grows as the speed grows.

recall.must_convey: That a falling raindrop is acted on by weight down, upthrust up, and a viscous drag up that grows with speed.
reject: F equals 6 pi eta r v

steps.memory_tip: Three forces on the raindrop: weight down, upthrust and drag up.

steps.label: Terminal velocity
lines: The drag keeps growing until it
balances weight minus upthrust:
After this the net force is zero
and the drop falls at a constant
terminal velocity
with ρ the drop's density and σ
the air's.
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Set drag equal to weight minus upthrust, then give v_t.
steps.why: Terminal velocity is the state of zero net force, not zero speed — the drop keeps moving, just without accelerating any further.
common_mistakes: Saying the raindrop stops; it keeps falling, at a constant speed.
Writing σ as the drop's density and ρ as the air's; it is the other way round.

recall.must_convey: That terminal velocity is reached when the drag balances weight minus upthrust, giving v t equals two ninths r squared g times rho minus sigma over eta.
accept: v t equals two ninths r squared g rho minus sigma over eta
reject: 6 pi eta r v is the drag alone

steps.memory_tip: v_t = (2/9)r²g(ρ − σ)/η — reached when drag balances weight minus upthrust.

steps.label: Why the impact speed is moderate
lines: Because of this, a raindrop does
not keep accelerating all the way
down. It reaches its terminal
velocity within a short fall and
then strikes the ground at that
steady, moderate speed rather than
at high speed.
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Say what the terminal velocity means for the raindrop's impact.
steps.why: This is the physical result the application is asked for — it explains why a small raindrop causes no harm even though it falls from a considerable height.
common_mistakes: Saying the raindrop accelerates all the way to the ground; it stops accelerating once terminal velocity is reached.
Leaving out why the terminal speed matters — the moderate impact.

recall.must_convey: That because of Stokes' law drag, a raindrop reaches a terminal velocity and so strikes the ground at a moderate speed, not at high speed.
reject: 6 pi eta r v is the formula

steps.memory_tip: Terminal velocity reached fast — that is why rain does not hurt.

insider_note: Four marks, four parts: the law and its formula, the three forces on the raindrop, the terminal-velocity balance, and why that keeps the impact speed moderate.
